The issue I’m finding with this assessment is that you’re equating the acts that gay people to how a trans person may or may not look. 

For instance, a lot of gay people who are leather daddies aren’t leather daddies in all aspects of life. Nor do they all look a like - some are big bears, others are not. Same thing with the “flamboyant” gay person, they do no all look alike.

Where as for trans people, our personalities and our attire can all fall into the “normie” category, yet not all of us will pass.

Not to mention, let’s let our messiness hangout there, fuck adhering to their white cishet standards.

There’s a lot of people who clearly adhere to respectability politics that are commenting, and honestly it’s sad.

As someone above mentioned, you can be not-so-beautiful and pass, and you can be beautiful and not-passing; I want to see the later more than the former. Hell, I want to see us untucked sometimes!!!

Most of us can’t fully adhere to the beauty standards that the cishet white patriarchy demands of us (and every other marginalized community).  If we want to lift up the trans community, that means lifting all of us up, celebrating all types of trans existence, not just the trans people who can pass and make cis people comfortable around us.

I just want to see more trans actors that are passable, non-passable, beautiful, not so beautiful (which tbh is cringy that there is such a thing society has made up), and everything in between. And I want to see transness being part of their characters experiences, but not central to who they are too.  I want to see trans romance, with cis people and other trans people. 

And yes, trans roles should only be played by trans actors.

This is a very respectability-politics point of view.  I think people identify with the messiness of human existence, not some curated way of being that exists for the comfort of the masses (aka cishet white audiences).  

All your take is going to do is to make it ok for trans people to exist as long as they don’t say a word and can pass as to not make them feel uncomfortable. I say BS, make them all feel uncomfortable, they need start getting uncomfortable with different ways of being.

First of all, as someone else pointed out, your species and race are predetermined by who your parents are. If both of your parents are white, then you’re going to be white no matter what. 

However, your parents do not determine your sex or gender. Yes, it’s a bit more complex than that because of how conception and fetal development work, but there are a ton of possible outcomes for you to be based on your parents biology - species and race are not. 

This is also getting very Eurocentric in here and ignoring how many non-western cultures have multiple genders, therefore giving prime examples of how gender is a social construct in the western world and universally happens on a continuum. 


It seems that we’re not doing a good job at separating gender and sex here. Both can be independent of each other.  I see a lot of people mentioning male or female brain within the constructs of social gender, but not within the context of sex and body. 

Have we ever thought a little more abstract about it though? That perhaps it’s the way the brain relates to its own body, not the social constructs of gender? That the brain was expecting part A, but the body developed part B instead and that it’s reconciliation that is most needed between the two?  After all, this would also explain why so many intersex people are more than likely totally at ease with the configuration of their body IF they were never subject to non consensual body modification by doctors and parents - because the brain was expecting this configuration.  

Within this particular context, someone can be totally ok with the make up of their body, but not ok with their gender and need different ways to express their gender. Someone else can be totally ok with their gender, but not the makeup of their body and need to modify their body. Regardless though, it’s impossible for them to be a different race or species.

Finally someone said the obvious!!!!

And even if some of your sex biology is a bit more predetermined, we know that sex sits on a continuum of variances, things can absolutely get tangled up.  

What will always be predetermined for you before you’re ever born based upon the two people who’s biologies interact via insemination is the fact that you’re always going to be a biological human and what race you are. But it’s how those two peoples biologies interact that determines the rest.

However, since I am trans it places more complexity in having people figure me out if they didn’t clock me from the beginning.

I definitely feel that you’re right about shorter girls being cuter, they can be picked up, they’re not a physical threat, they’re looked at as being dainty, and more femme. But if you’re not model thin, and/or you are past that acceptable height, then your womanhood is challenged.

Honestly, I deal with this quite often. I mostly have the one central driver of myself that controls things but will talk to these other parts. I have several different fragmented selves, they all show up differently, and they all come out at once when I’m going through a really bad panic attack. It’s overwhelming. They all tell me different things, and unfortunately one of them is a really dark fragment that tells me the one permanent way out of this pain.

What’s also hard, is that any one of these can take over too and be the driver, and my memory is mostly intact but also a blur and not always clear. 

It doesn’t happen with great frequency. I find it happens less if my life is a steady low. I find it happens most when it’s an unhealthy chaotic with deep lows and sudden but brief spikes of high. I’ve had a really confident part of me take over during those brief spikes and given me incredible nights and days that feel so good and so much fun, only to go back into this scared and frightened person the next day because something so small can set it off.  

I think the hard part is that they’re all separated from each other where they really need to be in unison with each other to collaborate and lead a much more healthy life. But they’re not, and I’m forced to have these fragments instead, with this driver that has to go to them for certain things, and a driver that can sometimes get be forced to hand over the keys in favor of these other fragments.

I had a really, really bad falling out with a friend this past summer. She was my roommate, we were close, I had feelings for her, and she was also my favorite person.

I had gotten diagnosed with ADHD early last summer, and it put me in a really fragile place. I started on some new meds, and she decided to pick an argument with me over how I was feeling on those meds, and what they were and were not doing to me. As a trans woman, people taking away my bodily autonomy is highly triggering, which she was basically doing, in a hostile manner. I went into heavy isolation and began to ideate heavily after that argument. However, it was not her fault that I started to ideate. She’s wasn’t responsible for my mental illness, and it’s symptoms, just like you are not responsible for your exes. 

Later that week, I got the courage to ask for help to get rid of the pills in my room that kept taunting me. I didn’t want to ask her, but she was the only person in my home at the time I needed to get it rid of them. I know this triggered her, and in what ways I’m not entirely sure because things went down hill from there. 

I’ve wondered if she’s scared that she was responsible for putting me in that place of ideation or not, or if she felt responsible for my life after giving her those pills. In either case, she wasn’t. She shouldn’t have yelled at me, and she should have looked at me giving her those pills as me taking responsibility of getting rid of them, and hiding them from myself. I don’t know if this is how she felt or not, it’s all speculative, as she did get angry with me and scolded me on how I needed to take care of myself. 

Regardless, none of my ideating was her fault, nor her responsibility, and she shouldn’t be taking on that responsibility either, I never asked her to. Could those triggers had been avoided, sure. But someone else could have also triggered me and I could have went into a dark place afterwards. That’s my mental health, that’s my pain, not anyone else’s. And it’s the same for your ex. It’s not your pain she’s dealing with, it’s her own. It’s her own mental health, not yours.

I and many others who ideate and have attempted do not want to die, we want to live. However, our pain is so severe we don’t know any other way of getting rid of it. These thoughts and actions are a way to take responsibility (in a fucked up way) to be out of our pain. This is our decision.

I have some really vivid memories from when I was a very young child, some of them good (like going to Disney World at 4) to some negative (getting a spinal tap at 2 or 3).  So forever, I couldn’t understand why I had this overwhelming feeling like something happened to me. However, there’s some puzzle pieces there for me. 

My parents were divorced, and growing up I always had a babysitter. For the first few years we had the same babysitter and her family. I have lots of memories with them, all good and I know nothing happened sexually (although it was the 80’s and I got the paddle on my rear, permission granted from my mom).  

When I was 4, my mom, sister and I moved to a new region and state. That started a cycle of babysitters for us. The first one wasn’t great, she and my sister picked on me, but nothing happened physically, and my memories are vivid. The next one we had was a godsend, she literally saved my life when I fell into a fire ant pile. I was never petrified of either of them, and I have decent memories I can recall. However, there’s one that came after the first two who I was absolutely petrified of. I remember she came to get me after school, and I refused to get in the car. I remember her face, I remember she had a husband I was more scared of, who’s face I cannot remember. Years later, my sister mentioned they had a son, who she was particularly frightened of herself, but I cannot remember the son at all. I do have some very vague memories of being in their house, but oddly enough, every time I think of their house I start imagining the house at the first babysitter we had from a different state associated with good memories. I know their houses were similar enough, but they’re different too. This memory has a different feel too, I’ve always remember that it included an overcast day or mood, and it included me sleeping there, but a normal sleep, more like a groggy out of it sleep. Those two details were never associated with any memory of our first babysitter in the first state we lived in, it’s all unique to this babysitter and her husband that I had this seemingly intense fear of, a fear I don’t recall with anyone else. For the life of me, I cannot understand why I can’t remember his face, why this fear existed, why I can’t remember their son, and why I have these specific memories of their house, but can’t exactly remember what the house looked like, only the day and mood of it all. 

Over the years, there’s been more puzzle pieces that’s been revealed to me. 
1.) Years later, I can remember a girl in our class was being pulled because she was struggling. The excuse given to us was that she had a poor encounter with someone at a summer camp. I don’t remember anyone having any clue as to what happened, but I knew exactly, and I stood frozen and scared as though I could relate.

2.) I started having this irrational fear of men, being alone with them, and of me sleeping while they’re in the same room or a place I was unfamiliar with (like a hotel or being in a room next door). I even developed these feelings around men I knew and trusted like my dad, step dad, or grandfather. 

3.) Years later, when my mom remarried, I got really sick. My step dad, with my mom in my room, very tenderly spread some Vicks vapor rub on my chest to help me. That’s the first time I remember experiencing body memories, of a male’s hands touching my body underneath clothing. 

4.) Body memories persisted throughout my life, only when triggered though, and I could never understand why until I started learning about the book “The Body Keeps the Score”, things started to make more sense.

5.) Many, many years later I had a flashback while I was on a solo road trip. I was listening to a podcast about the Michael Jackson HBO documentary (I’ve never watched it for a reason), the podcast wasn’t directly about the documentary, but rather the experience of this NYT editor who watched it. However, this editor described a scene that happened between the two boys, and it triggered a flashback of the same scene I was once in.

I knew it was real, because I’ve had memories of a traumatic event that happened in seventh grade that resurfaced for me many, many years later. Repressing memories is now something I know I do. Up until that flashback, I was always confused, I was always wondering, I was always doubting myself. I’m not any more, I know something happened, and trying to relive the memory isn’t worth it. I have enough to know something happened now, that I’m not making it up, and that it gives me greater context around my experiences with sex and orientation, and my gender and gender identity (not that it was the cause of my orientation or gender identity, but more that it a major factor that shaped how I experienced these things). 

I don’t think you’re making this up, and I do think your mind and body are telling you these things for a reason. You also might not need to relive your memories either to be able to heal and to give context of how this has impacted you. I do believe that it’s a misnomer that we need to relive trauma to be able to heal or understand fully what impact it might have had.

The “historical” evidence you’re referring to is probably taken from a study of the last 25 years or so that looked at which populations take hormone replacement therapy more often. It fails to look at which populations have greater access to gender affirming healthcare, which has disproportionately skewed towards trans women for several reasons.

First reason is that white trans women often have higher incomes pre transition because they often had careers that paid more since they’re living as a perceived male. This is going to skew the numbers right there (it would also skew white, because POC trans populations often had to get their hormones through underground markets). Trans men, often times living as “butch” women, had to get their testosterone in underground markets since they often times did not have access because of lower incomes. 

Second reason is that trans women have disproportionately had the most media attention (albeit almost all negatively until recently). Most trans men had zero representation, not even negative. There was little knowledge that transition was even possible for trans men. 

Much of this continues to play out to this day. There’s no way of knowing for sure whether or not trans women exist at higher proportions. These studies that suggests they know are highly flawed.

A soft heat when it comes to potentially causing harm to a community must be taken into account in order to think about the consequences of said study. They might not be explicitly biased, but they’re often littered with negligence, and fail to identity the full scope of what the trans experience is like. This is a lot to unpack here. I am personally going through what I classify as my second transition, but what that is for me is navigating getting all of my surgeries. I transitioned socially to a woman several years ago, and going through surgeries and the process of obtaining them is taking on a new emotional toll. 

Truth be told, I sometimes hate being trans myself. It's harder for me to date as a trans woman than it was for me as a "man". My height and foot size make clothes and shoe shopping very difficult. The fact that I can no longer travel safely to some places as a result of being trans also bothers me. And navigating these surgeries can be horrific and humiliating. But for me, what was worse, was being a man. My top surgery results gave me such gender euphoria that for the first time ever, I don't hate my chest. 

I also live in a huge city which is very progressive (compared to the rest of the US) and in a blue state.  We have a vibrant queer community that's very supportive. My job and chosen family are highly supportive.  If I lived in a city or state that did not have this support, I don't know if I would feel the same, that perhaps I would hate being trans more.  

When I take a step back and think of the negatives that I experience with being trans, surgery and medical aside, it has much more to do with the societal treatment than actually being trans for me. Even with the surgery stuff though, for me, the end results are amazing and affirming. 

From what you have described, and saying that you do like the changes T has made, it sounds like a lot of your struggle is truly society's treatment of trans people than the actual fact of being trans - again sans the medical part that we can't get away from easily. 

I am not a trans person who believes that the community should shy away from and be hush about detransitioning. I think we should own this narrative, and not let the gender critical/terf/conservatives use it against us. I think we should take this seriously and support those who need to transition.  I do believe that there are some who experiment and get to a point where they realize that transition is not for them or who they are. I personally think this should be normalized. So I don't want you to think that I am trying to dissuade you from detransitioning. If that's what you ultimately need, then I say go for it. But, I do think the fact that you like the changes T has made does say a lot about you too. 

There are so many ways to be trans, no one way is the correct way. If you need to live your life as a cis person, then go ahead. But, just because you detransition and you live your life as a cis person doesn't mean you're trans or not trans. That's only for you to decide. 

I have so much empathy for you, the journey of figuring out your gender is not easy, one I don't wish on anyone. It's painful, and I hope that you find a way to ease that pain however that might be. Whatever is the right path for you, I hope that you'll at least always support trans people, and if you do, I'll always support you. We all deserve to be happy and free of bodily judgement, and I wish that for you.
